narrative: The model estimated a 94% chance that you will leave your job, which is why the promotion was denied: it treated you as a very high retention risk, not as someone lacking ability. The strongest signal was your total work experience of six to ten years; compared with the one-to-five-year group that makes up most employees predicted to stay, this longer record suggested greater mobility. Second was your one-to-five years in the current organization, which the model associated with leaving rather than staying. Third was that you reported other job opportunities; most employees predicted to stay reported none, so this sharply increased the leave prediction. All three top factors pushed the prediction toward leaving, and together they outweighed signals pointing toward staying. Before revisiting promotion, your manager should discuss your career path, promotion criteria, and outside options openly, and review practical retention levers such as recognition, support, workload, and compensation. You should ask for specific feedback and a development plan, while the organization should treat this as a retention conversation rather than a final judgment.
